vsm1.1:98.0: The Method of Achieving the Fourfold Purification
vsm1.1:98.1: 98. (a) So, in this fourfold virtue, Pātimokkha restraint has to be undertaken by means of faith.
vsm1.1:98.2: For that is accomplished by faith, since the announcing of training precepts is outside the disciples’ province;
vsm1.1:98.3: and the evidence here is the refusal of the request to allow disciples to announce training precepts (see Vin III 9–10).
vsm1.1:98.4:
Having therefore undertaken through faith the training precepts without exception as announced,
one should completely perfect them without regard for life.
vsm1.1:98.5:
For this is said: “As a hen guards her eggs, Or as a yak her tail, Or like a darling child, Or like an only eye—
So you who are engaged Your virtue to protect, Be prudent at all times And ever scrupulous.” (Source untraced)
vsm1.1:98.6: Also it is said further: “So too, sire, when a training precept for disciples is announced by me,
vsm1.1:98.7: my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of life” (A IV 201).
vsm1.1:99.1: 99. And the story of the elders bound by robbers in the forest should be understood in this sense.
vsm1.1:99.2: It seems that robbers in the Mahāvaṭṭanī Forest bound an elder with black creepers and made him lie down.
vsm1.1:99.3:
While he lay there for seven days he augmented his insight, and after reaching
the fruition of non-return, he died there and was reborn in the Brahmā-world.
vsm1.1:99.4: Also they bound another elder in Tambapaṇṇi Island (Sri Lanka) with string creepers and made him lie down.
vsm1.1:99.5: When a forest fire came and the creepers were not cut, he established insight and attained Nibbāna simultaneously with his death.
vsm1.1:99.6:
When the Elder Abhaya, a preacher of the Dīgha Nikāya, passed by with five hundred bhikkhus,
he saw what had happened and he had the elder’s body cremated and a shrine built.
vsm1.1:99.7:
Therefore let other clansmen also: Maintain the rules of conduct pure, Renouncing life if there be need,
Rather than break virtue’s restraint By the World’s Saviour decreed.
vsm1.1:100.1: 100. (b) And as Pātimokkha restraint is undertaken out of faith,
vsm1.1:100.2: so restraint of the sense faculties should be undertaken with mindfulness.
vsm1.1:100.3: For that is accomplished by mindfulness,
vsm1.1:100.4:
because when the sense faculties’ functions are founded on mindfulness,
there is no liability to invasion by covetousness and the rest.
vsm1.1:100.5:
So, recollecting the Fire Discourse, which begins thus, “Better, bhikkhus, the extirpation of the eye faculty by a red-hot burning
blazing glowing iron spike than the apprehension of signs in the particulars of visible objects cognizable by the eye” (S IV 168),
vsm1.1:100.6:
this restraint should be properly undertaken by preventing with unremitting mindfulness any apprehension, in the objective
fields consisting of visible data, etc., of any signs, etc., likely to encourage covetousness,
etc., to invade consciousness occurring in connection with the eye door, and so on.
vsm1.1:101.1: 101. When not undertaken thus, virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is unenduring: it does not last,
vsm1.1:101.2: like a crop not fenced in with branches.
vsm1.1:101.3: And it is raided by the robber defilements as a village with open gates is by thieves.
vsm1.1:101.4: And lust leaks into his mind as rain does into a badly-roofed house.
vsm1.1:101.5:
For this is said: “Among the visible objects, sounds, and smells, And tastes, and tangibles, guard the faculties; For when
these doors are open and unguarded, Then thieves will come and raid as ’twere a village (?). And just as with an ill-roofed
house The rain comes leaking in, so too Will lust come leaking in for sure Upon an undeveloped mind” (Dhp 13).
vsm1.1:102.1: 102. When it is undertaken thus, virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is enduring: it lasts, like a crop well fenced in with branches.
vsm1.1:102.2: And it is not raided by the robber defilements, as a village with well-guarded gates is not by thieves.
vsm1.1:102.3: And lust does not leak into his mind, as rain does not into a well-roofed house.
vsm1.1:102.4:
For this is said: “Among the visible objects, sounds and smells, And tastes and tangibles, guard the faculties; For when
these doors are closed and truly guarded, Thieves will not come and raid as ’twere a village (?). “And just as with a well-roofed
house No rain comes leaking in, so too No lust comes leaking in for sure Upon a well-developed mind” (Dhp 14).
vsm1.1:103.1: 103. This, however, is the teaching at its very highest.
vsm1.1:103.2: This mind is called “quickly transformed” (A I 10),
vsm1.1:103.3:
so restraint of the faculties should be undertaken by removing arisen lust with the contemplation of foulness,
as was done by the Elder Vaṅgīsa soon after he had gone forth.
vsm1.1:103.4: As the elder was wandering for alms, it seems, soon after going forth, lust arose in him on seeing a woman.
vsm1.1:103.5:
Thereupon he said to the venerable Ānanda: “I am afire with sensual lust. And burning flames consume
my mind; In pity tell me, Gotama, How to extinguish it for good” (S I 188).
vsm1.1:103.6:
The elder said: “You do perceive mistakenly, That burning flames consume your mind. Look for no sign of beauty there, For that it
is which leads to lust. See foulness there and keep your mind Harmoniously concentrated; Formations see as alien,
As ill, not self, so this great lust May be extinguished, and no more Take fire thus ever and again” (S I 188).
vsm1.1:103.7: The elder expelled his lust and then went on with his alms round.
vsm1.1:104.1:
104. Moreover, a bhikkhu who is fulfilling restraint of the faculties should be like the Elder Cittagutta
resident in the Great Cave at Kuraṇḍaka, and like the Elder Mahā Mitta resident at the Great Monastery of Coraka.
vsm1.1:105.1: 105. In the Great Cave of Kuraṇḍaka, it seems, there was a lovely painting of the Renunciation of the Seven Buddhas.
vsm1.1:105.2: A number of bhikkhus wandering about among the dwellings saw the painting and said, “What a lovely painting, venerable sir!”
vsm1.1:105.3:
The elder said: “For more than sixty years, friends, I have lived in the cave, and I
did not know whether there was any painting there or not.
vsm1.1:105.4: Now, today, I know it through those who have eyes.”
vsm1.1:105.5: The elder, it seems, though he had lived there for so long, had never raised his eyes and looked up at the cave.
vsm1.1:105.6: And at the door of his cave there was a great ironwood tree.
vsm1.1:105.7: And the elder had never looked up at that either.
vsm1.1:105.8: He knew it was in flower when he saw its petals on the ground each year.
vsm1.1:106.1:
106. The king heard of the elder’s great virtues, and he sent for him three times,
desiring to pay homage to him. When the elder did not go,
vsm1.1:106.2:
he had the breasts of all the women with infants in the town bound and sealed off,
saying “As long as the elder does not come let the children go without milk,”
vsm1.1:106.3: Out of compassion for the children the elder went to Mahāgāma.
vsm1.1:106.4:
When the king heard that he had come, he said “Go and bring the elder in. I shall take the precepts.”
Having had him brought up into the inner palace, he paid homage to him and provided him with a meal.
vsm1.1:106.5: Then, saying, “Today, venerable sir, there is no opportunity. I shall take the precepts tomorrow,” he took the elder’s bowl.
vsm1.1:106.6: After following him for a little, he paid homage with the queen and turned back.
vsm1.1:106.7: As seven days went by thus, whether it was the king who paid homage or whether it was the queen,
vsm1.1:106.8: the elder said, “May the king be happy.”
vsm1.1:107.1: 107. Bhikkhus asked: “Why is it, venerable sir,
vsm1.1:107.2: that whether it is the king who pays the homage or the queen you say ‘May the king be happy’?”
vsm1.1:107.3: The elder replied: “Friends, I do not notice whether it is the king or the queen.”
vsm1.1:107.4:
At the end of seven days when it was found that the elder was not happy living there, he was dismissed by the king.
He went back to the Great Cave at Kuraṇḍaka. When it was night he went out onto his walk.
vsm1.1:107.5: A deity who dwelt in the ironwood tree stood by with a torch of sticks.
vsm1.1:107.6: Then his meditation subject became quite clear and plain.
vsm1.1:107.7:
The elder, thinking “How clear my meditation subject is today!” was glad, and immediately after
the middle watch he reached Arahantship, making the whole rock resound.
vsm1.1:108.1:
108. So when another clansman seeks his own good: Let him not be hungry-eyed, Like a monkey in the groves,
Like a wild deer in the woods, Like a nervous little child. Let him go with eyes downcast Seeing
a plough yoke’s length before, That he fall not in the power Of the forest-monkey mind.
vsm1.1:109.1: 109. The Elder Mahā Mitta’s mother was sick with a poisoned tumour.
vsm1.1:109.2: She told her daughter, who as a bhikkhunī had also gone forth,
vsm1.1:109.3: “Lady, go to your brother. Tell him my trouble and bring back some medicine.”
vsm1.1:109.5:
The elder said: “I do not know how to gather root medicines and such things and concoct
a medicine from them. But rather I will tell you a medicine:
vsm1.1:109.6:
since I went forth I have not broken my virtue of restraint of the sense
faculties by looking at the bodily form of the opposite sex with a lustful mind.
vsm1.1:109.7: By this declaration of truth may my mother get well. Go and tell the lay devotee and rub her body.”
vsm1.1:109.8: She went and told her what had happened and then did as she had been instructed.
vsm1.1:109.9: At that very moment the lay devotee’s tumour vanished, shrinking away like a lump of froth.
vsm1.1:109.10:
She got up and uttered a cry of joy: “If the Fully Enlightened One were still alive,
why should he not stroke with his netadorned hand the head of a bhikkhu like my son?”
vsm1.1:110.1: 110. Let another noble clansman Gone forth in the Dispensation Keep, as did the Elder Mitta, Perfect faculty restraint.
vsm1.1:111.1: 111. (c) As restraint of the faculties is to be undertaken by means of mindfulness,
vsm1.1:111.2: so livelihood purification is to be undertaken by means of energy.
vsm1.1:111.3: For that is accomplished by energy, because the abandoning of wrong livelihood is effected in one who has rightly applied energy.
vsm1.1:111.4:
Abandoning, therefore, unbefitting wrong search, this should be undertaken with energy by means of the right
kind of search consisting in going on alms round, etc.,
vsm1.1:111.5: avoiding what is of impure origin as though it were a poisonous snake, and using only requisites of pure origin.
vsm1.1:112.1:
112. Herein, for one who has not taken up the ascetic practices, any requisites
obtained from the Community, from a group of bhikkhus,
vsm1.1:112.2: or from laymen who have confidence in his special qualities of teaching the Dhamma, etc., are called “of pure origin.”
vsm1.1:112.3: But those obtained on alms round, etc., are of extremely pure origin.
vsm1.1:112.4:
For one who has taken up the ascetic practices, those obtained on alms round, etc., and—as long as this is in accordance with the
rules of the ascetic practices—from people who have confidence in his special qualities of asceticism, are called “of pure origin.”
vsm1.1:112.5:
And if he has got putrid urine with mixed gall nuts and “four-sweets” for the purpose of curing a certain
affliction, and he eats only the broken gall nuts, thinking, “Other companions in the life of purity
will eat the ‘four-sweets’,” his undertaking of the ascetic practices is befitting,
vsm1.1:112.6: for he is then called a bhikkhu who is supreme in the Noble Ones’ heritages (A II 28).
